title: Organizing Meetings Around Questions Instead of Topics
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece argues that the standard, topic-driven meeting agenda quietly suppresses debate because topics sit passively on the page and rarely demand a response. Reframing each agenda item as a genuine question, the author argues, forces sharper thinking from the leader in advance and invites more active participation once the meeting starts. A worked example shows how a vague topic like 'Improving the Culture' can become a much more provocative question that presumes an end state or a root cause. The piece closes by noting that question-driven agendas also make off-topic discussion easier to spot and redirect, since anything that isn't an answer to the question stands out as irrelevant.
points: Topic-driven agendas tend to sit passively on the page and don't demand engagement.
Reframing agenda items as questions forces leaders to clarify what they actually want to address.
A vague topic like 'Improving the Culture' becomes sharper as a specific, provocative question.
Sending questions in advance primes participants and keeps the resulting discussion on track.
quotes: A simple way to promote more discussion and to get people excited and ready to contribute is to cast each topic or issue as a question.
The best agenda questions pose a challenge, presume an end state, or suggest a root cause.
Meetings, agendas, and topics organized by questions create a more vibrant dialogue between team members.
That’s because any point that is not an answer to the question becomes obvious and can be brushed aside as irrelevant.
Effective meetings are driven by agendas and often include a variety of issues, topics, and discussion points.
Naturally, leaders organize meetings topic-by-topic to keep the discussions focused and on track.
Look at virtually any meeting agenda at nearly any enterprise, and you will find a topic or issue-driven agenda.
While there is nothing wrong or problematic with this well-worn approach, it has one Achilles heel: it doesn’t promote dialogue or intense debate unless the topic is highly charged for team members.
